subject: Art & Design
title: CMYK vs. RGB: Screen to Print
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on CMYK vs. RGB: Screen to Print.

hook.text: You design a vibrant poster on screen. It prints dull and muddy. Welcome to the RGB-to-CMYK gap.

buildup.text: RGB is additive (light). CMYK is subtractive (ink). They produce color through opposite physics.

discovery.text: RGB's gamut is wider — it can display neon greens and electric blues that CMYK simply cannot print.

twist.text: Designing in RGB for print is the #1 beginner mistake. Always convert early and check soft proofs.

climax.text: Professional designers work in the target color space from the start to avoid nasty surprises.

punchline.text: What glows on screen doesn't always survive the printer.

quiz.question: Why do colors often look duller in print than on screen?
options: CMYK ink has a smaller color range than RGB light

details.summary: RGB (red, green, blue) is additive — mixing light for screens. CMYK (cyan, magenta, yellow, black) is subtractive — mixing inks for print. Vibrant screen colors often look dull when printed because CMYK's gamut is smaller than RGB's.
details.whyItMatters: The most common color disappointment in design happens when a vibrant screen design prints as a dull version. Understanding the RGB-CMYK gap prevents wasted print runs, client disappointment, and costly reprints.
takeaways: RGB adds light for screens; CMYK subtracts light with inks
CMYK's color range is smaller than RGB's
Converting and proofing prevents print disappointment

faq.question: Why can't printers reproduce all screen colors?
faq.answer: Screens emit light directly into your eyes, achieving vivid colors. Inks absorb light from paper and reflect what remains — a physically limited process. Bright neon greens, electric blues, and vivid oranges on screen have no CMYK equivalent. Spot colors like Pantone can extend the range.

faq.question: Should I design in CMYK from the start for print?
faq.answer: Many designers work in RGB for wider creative freedom, then convert to CMYK for print production. But designing in CMYK from the start prevents surprise color shifts. Key: always check how your colors look in CMYK before finalizing any design intended for print.
